# Chub Mackerel Price Dynamics, Interannual Size Variation, and Ocean–Market Linkages Across Pacific Rim Markets

The strongest evidence supports a qualified conclusion. Chub mackerel prices do respond to supply, grade composition, trade demand, and market structure, but no harmonized, species-specific monthly price panel currently permits a defensible Pacific Rim-wide ranking. South Korea provides the best integrated case: Busan auction data show large price differences among size grades, a growing share of small-fish landings, and an export-driven reorganization of fishing activity. Japan and the United States provide useful official port or landed-price series, but their readily available records are often aggregate, provisional, or not fully comparable. China, Russia, Mexico, Chile, and Peru have important fisheries or trade flows, yet the supplied evidence does not provide equivalent chub-mackerel price series at matching market levels.

Biological variation is clearer than price comparability. Northwest Pacific assessments show time-varying weight at age and a recent decline in the weights of older fish, while high-seas length-frequency data show annual asymptotic fork lengths ranging from 39.4 to 46.0 cm during 2019–2024. Korean landed fork length has remained small and fluctuating rather than showing a statistically significant population-wide decline. The Korean evidence indicates that fishing-ground choice, gear selectivity, market sorting, and a strong young-fish component may explain much of the observed small-fish catch, although a decline in size at age cannot be excluded.

Oceanographic mechanisms are well supported at the biological level. Kuroshio–Oyashio circulation, fronts, temperature, chlorophyll-a, prey fields, marine heatwaves, and climate variability influence larval transport, growth, recruitment, distribution, condition, and biomass. Some relationships have measurable lags of one to three years. The evidence becomes much weaker at the final step from environment to price: environmental conditions affect supply and quality, but direct environment-to-price coefficients for comparable Pacific Rim chub-mackerel markets are not available. The most defensible interpretation is therefore a chain of linked associations, not a single demonstrated causal correlation.

This report first defines the taxon, stocks, products, markets, and geographic boundaries. It then compares price evidence, measures interannual size and weight variation, explains the oceanographic mechanisms, connects biological quality to fishery economics, and evaluates the available correlations while distinguishing observation, model output, and causation. It closes with a country-by-country evidence comparison and practical implications for monitoring and management.

## Species, stocks, markets, and geographic scope

### Taxonomic definition

Chub mackerel is *Scomber japonicus*, also called Pacific chub mackerel or, in some North American management documents, Pacific mackerel. It is a pelagic scombrid distributed through temperate and subtropical waters. The North Pacific Fisheries Commission identifies common names including masaba in Japan, godeungeo in Korea, Taiyu in China, and Japanese mackerel in Russia ([NPFC species summary](https://www.npfc.int/system/files/2024-01/NPFC-2024-TWG%20CMSA08-WP02%20Species%20summary%20for%20chub%20mackerel.pdf)).

The principal taxonomic problem is confusion with spotted or blue mackerel, *Scomber australasicus*. Commercial records frequently group both under “mackerel,” “saba,” or an unspecified frozen-mackerel code. They are biologically and commercially related but should not automatically be pooled. In the East China Sea, Japanese catch statistics and biometric samples distinguish the two species; female maturity occurred at approximately 275 mm fork length for *S. japonicus* and 310 mm for *S. australasicus*, while the mature-fish temperature ranges were approximately 15–22°C and 17–25°C, respectively ([Yukami et al.](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12562-008-0015-7)). Larval studies likewise found *S. japonicus* in a cooler, broader 15–22°C habitat and *S. australasicus* in a warmer, narrower 20–23°C habitat ([Sassa and Tsukamoto](https://doi.org/10.3354/meps08832)).

This distinction matters directly for price analysis. A country may appear to have a higher or lower “mackerel price” because its series contains a different species mix, size distribution, frozen product, or market level. The problem is especially serious for customs codes such as HS 030374 or HS 030354, which identify frozen mackerel categories but do not necessarily identify *S. japonicus*.

### Stock units

Two principal stock usages are recognized in the Northwest Pacific:

- The Tsushima Current stock occurs in the East China Sea, Yellow Sea, Sea of Japan, Korean waters, and western Japanese waters.
- The Pacific stock spawns mainly around the Izu Islands and migrates northward toward Sanriku, eastern Hokkaido, the Kuril region, and adjacent high seas.

The distinction is partly biological and operational rather than based on clear genetic separation. The NPFC describes the Pacific stock as a straddling stock harvested in Japanese and Russian national waters and in the NPFC Convention Area ([NPFC 2025 assessment](https://www.npfc.int/system/files/2026-04/Stock%20assessment%20report%20for%20chub%20mackerel%202025.pdf)). The Tsushima Current stock is jointly used by China, Japan, and South Korea, but the countries fish it in different seasons and areas. Chinese fishing is concentrated mainly from July to December, whereas Japanese and Korean exploitation is more concentrated in winter ([stock-comparison study](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2022.996626/full)).

The northeastern Pacific is a separate management case. U.S. and Mexican authorities manage *S. japonicus* north of Punta Abreojos, Baja California, as one transboundary unit, although stock structure is not definitively known. The range extends from southeastern Alaska to Banderas Bay, Mexico, including the Gulf of California ([Jensen et al. 2025](https://www.pcouncil.org/documents/2025/05/catch-only-stock-assessment-of-pacific-mackerel-scomber-japonicus-for-u-s-management-in-the-2025-26-and-2026-27-fishing-years.pdf/)). A long-term assumption that approximately 70% of the stock resides in U.S. waters is embedded in the U.S. harvest-control rule; that is a management assumption, not a directly observed annual distribution.

Chile and Peru require special caution. Their major “jack mackerel” fishery is *Trachurus murphyi*, not *S. japonicus*. Chilean production statistics list 556,494 tonnes of jack mackerel and 86,045 tonnes of Pacific chub mackerel in 2020, confirming that the two are separate statistical entries ([FAO GLOBEFISH Chile profile](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/1429d540-6834-4b32-8ced-1eeb852b5119/content)). Peruvian reports also distinguish *T. murphyi* from *S. japonicus*, but their detailed biological and market evidence is dominated by jack mackerel ([Peru annual report](https://sprfmo.int/assets/Meetings/02-SC/13th-SC-2025/Ecosystems/SC13-ECO05-Abundance-and-biological-aspects-of-Jack-mackerel-and-other-species-of-the-Peru-Current-in-the-Humboldt-System.pdf)). Jack-mackerel values cannot be used as chub-mackerel values.

### Market and geographic selection

The most informative Pacific Rim panel is therefore not a single homogeneous market but a set of linked cases:

| Case | Biological unit | Main reason for inclusion | Main evidence type |
|---|---|---|---|
| Japan | Pacific and Tsushima Current uses of *S. japonicus*; sometimes combined with *S. australasicus* | Major harvester, consumer, processor, and importer | Port prices, catches, size sampling, stock assessments |
| South Korea | Mainly Tsushima Current *S. japonicus* | Strongest grade-resolved auction, export, catch-price, and market evidence | Busan auction, retail, export, biological sampling |
| China | Mixed *S. japonicus* and *S. australasicus* in some records; high-seas *S. japonicus* can be modeled separately | Major harvester, processor, exporter, and importer | Logbooks, CPUE, trade benchmarks, habitat studies |
| Russia | NPFC *S. japonicus* catch is reported as nearly species-pure since 2014, but domestic price reports often concern Atlantic mackerel | Important Northwest Pacific harvester and regional market | NPFC catch and gear data; Russian market monitoring |
| United States–Mexico | Northeastern Pacific *S. japonicus* management unit | Transboundary eastern-Pacific fishery | Stock assessments and U.S. landed prices |
| Chile–Peru | *S. japonicus* is present but *T. murphyi* dominates many market and fishery records | Pacific Rim context and species-classification check | Production, landings, and jack-mackerel reports |

The market levels are not interchangeable. A landing or ex-vessel price is paid close to the fishery; an auction price reflects grading and first sale; a wholesale price includes storage, handling, and distribution; a retail price includes downstream margins; and a customs unit value is the declared trade value divided by quantity. Import and export values also use different valuation conventions. NOAA, for example, notes that U.S. export values are free-alongside-ship while import values are customs values ([NOAA foreign fishery trade data](https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/national/sustainable-fisheries/foreign-fishery-trade-data)).

Product form is equally important. Mackerel may be sold fresh whole, frozen whole round, headed and gutted, filleted, canned, or processed into portions. Frozen-mackerel trade overviews commonly combine Atlantic mackerel, chub mackerel, and blue mackerel, with whole-round and headed-and-gutted products as major forms ([Tridge frozen-mackerel specification](https://www.tridge.com/market-overview/frozen-mackerel)). A price comparison is meaningful only when species, form, grade, size band, market level, currency, and unit are aligned.

### Time windows and measurement conventions

The biological and market time scales are different:

- The NPFC assessment covers fishing years FY1970–FY2023, with a July–June fishing-year definition.
- Member catch-at-length coverage is strongest from 2014 or 2016 onward, depending on country and variable.
- Japan has much longer length and catch sampling, including approximately 60,000 annual length records in its Pacific-coast assessment system.
- The Korean Busan auction series covers 2014–2025.
- Korean catch-dependent pricing uses monthly data from July 2017 through June 2022.
- The high-seas LBB series covers April–December 2019–2024.
- U.S. and Mexican assessment data generally cover 2008–2024, but the supplied evidence does not provide a comparable price series.
- Visible Tridge country benchmarks cover October 2025–March 2026, with later months hidden.
- The evidence cutoff for this report is 13 September 2026. A PacFIN CPS002 report run on 15 September 2026 is therefore labeled as outside the cutoff and is not used for cutoff-bounded conclusions.

Prices are reported in the original currencies unless explicitly noted: Japanese yen per kilogram, Korean won per kilogram or per fish, Russian rubles per kilogram, U.S. dollars per pound or kilogram, and trade values in U.S. dollars. Korean auction prices were also deflated with a 2020 CPI base. A real-price conversion has the general form:

$$P^{real}_t=P^{nominal}_t\left(\frac{CPI_{base}}{CPI_t}\right).$$

There is no supplied cross-country dataset applying the same deflator, exchange-rate convention, product definition, and market level to all countries. Cross-country numerical rankings must therefore remain conditional.

## Chub mackerel price dynamics in Pacific Rim markets

### What can and cannot be compared

The evidence falls into three tiers.

The first tier is species-linked, market-specific evidence. South Korea’s Busan auction data are the strongest example because they identify *S. japonicus*, distinguish commercial grades, provide prices and quantities, and link transactions to fishing grounds. The Korean catch-dependent price study is also useful because it uses monthly chub-mackerel catch and price data rather than a broad frozen-mackerel category.

The second tier consists of official but taxonomically or commercially broader records. Japan’s “saba” series, Russian Atlantic-mackerel prices, and U.S. landed-price reports are useful for market behavior but do not always isolate the target taxon and stock. They should be used as country-specific indicators rather than pooled prices.

The third tier consists of international frozen-mackerel benchmarks and customs unit values. These are valuable for trade direction, substitution, and supply shocks, but they combine species, forms, grades, and destinations. Their proper interpretation is market context, not a chub-mackerel price index.

### South Korea: the most complete market case

#### Grade and auction prices

The Busan Cooperative Fish Market series covers 2014–2025 and captures 98.9% of the chub-mackerel weight auctioned there from the large purse-seine fleet. It represents a single market rather than a national census, covering 68.4% of national large-purse-seine production over the period, with annual coverage ranging from 59.8% to 79.2% ([Yoo and Yoon](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2026.1945408/full)).

The four commercial grades are strongly differentiated by size and market channel:

| Grade | Mean fork length | Mean weight | 2024 auction price | Main channel |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | 36.8 cm | 694 g | 9,752 KRW/kg | Domestic food |
| 2 | 34.5 cm | 543 g | 6,503 KRW/kg | Domestic food |
| 3 | 31.8 cm | 403 g | 3,576 KRW/kg | Mostly domestic food |
| 4 | 27.6 cm | 251 g | 1,355 KRW/kg | Export, canning, or feed |

The 2024 Grade 1 price was therefore approximately seven times the Grade 4 price, but this is a grade and market-channel difference, not a pure causal estimate of the price effect of biological size. Grade 4 averages 27.6 cm and 251 g; 83% of fish in that grade are below the approximately 30 cm export or canning threshold, and 25% are below the approximately 200 g feed threshold. Grade 3 averages 31.8 cm and 403 g, with 83% at or above 30 cm and therefore more likely to enter the domestic food channel.

This distinction explains why “small fish” and “low-quality fish” should not be treated as synonyms. Size is commercially decisive, while condition, lipid content, freshness, oxidation, and cold-chain history are separate quality attributes. A small fish may have a stable export outlet and good freshness but still command a low price per kilogram because it serves a different channel.

Grade 4’s real price increased from 1,120 to 1,743 KRW/kg in 2020 prices over 2014–2025, with a Mann–Kendall trend test of p = 0.03. The increase was not a small-fish premium. In 2025, Grade 1 rose from 9,752 to 13,327 KRW/kg, a 37% nominal increase, while Grade 4 rose by 50%; the Grade 4-to-Grade 1 price ratio changed from 0.16 to 0.15, remaining within its historical 0.12–0.25 range. The common price movement is more consistent with a general market shock or rising demand than with a new quality premium for small fish.

#### Export demand and fishing-ground relocation

Reported Korean chub-mackerel exports rose from 22.6 thousand tonnes valued at US$28 million in 2014 to 144.2 thousand tonnes valued at US$200 million in 2025. Over the same period, Grade 4’s share of fleet revenue rose from 47% to 89%. The association between Grade 4 revenue share and export value was strong in raw levels, Spearman ρ = 0.69, p = 0.014. It weakened to ρ = 0.29, p = 0.35 after detrending and became −0.04 in first differences ([Yoo and Yoon](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2026.1945408/full)).

The statistical progression is important:

1. Raw levels moved together over a decade.
2. Detrending removed most of the association.
3. Year-to-year changes did not move together.

The raw correlation therefore does not establish that exports caused the annual Grade 4 revenue share. It is consistent with a lagged and inventory-mediated trade system in which fish are frozen, accumulated, and shipped after landing. The Grade 4 landing volume itself had almost no year-to-year association with export volume, ρ = 0.03, p = 0.91.

The spatial evidence nevertheless makes the market interpretation plausible. In winter 2025, the Southern East Sea accounted for 83.8% of the catch, compared with 0–36.7% in each of the previous ten winters. The fleet operated an average of 117 km from Busan, compared with 402 km in 2022 and 253 km in 2024. The Southern East Sea catch was 97.0% Grade 4, compared with 75.3% outside the region, based on 4,865 transactions from 21 vessels.

This is a coherent economic mechanism: once an export market can absorb large volumes of small fish, the fleet’s return from a nearby small-fish ground can improve even if the price per kilogram remains far below that of large fish. The evidence does not prove that export demand caused the relocation. A strong young cohort or changing fish availability could have drawn the fleet to the same grounds. It does show that the market change and the spatial change point in the same direction.

#### Catch-dependent pricing

A separate South Korean study used monthly catch and price data from July 2017 through June 2022. Catch was measured in tonnes and price in 1,000 won per tonne. Logarithmic, rational, and irrational catch-dependent price functions produced R² values of 0.724, 0.757, and 0.769, respectively, with all fitted parameters significant at p < 0.05 ([Jang and Cho](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13662-025-03898-9)).

The fitted functions implied that prices were above the sample average when monthly catch was below approximately 13,000 tonnes for the logarithmic model, 16,600 tonnes for the rational model, and 14,600 tonnes for the irrational model. The logarithmic function became particularly sensitive when catch exceeded roughly 15,000 tonnes.

These are useful conditional estimates, not structural demand elasticities. The study assumed that demand was sufficiently stable and did not model changing export destinations, inventories, imports, exchange rates, or market competition. The high R² values show that catch explains much of the observed monthly price variation within the Korean sample under the selected functional forms; they do not show that a change in catch alone would produce the same response outside that period.

The study’s simulations also demonstrate how price formation changes harvest incentives. Over a simulated ten-year horizon, the rational pricing scenario generated the highest average profit, 16.51 billion won. The logarithmic scenario generated the lowest average catch, 12,424 tonnes, and profit, 15.35 billion won, but the highest total biomass, 189,967 tonnes, and the lowest average effort, 0.0683. These are model projections using constant unit effort costs and stable demand assumptions, not observed outcomes.

The same model found that a July closure immediately after spawning produced the largest simulated resource recovery, 6–8%, with a 2–5% profit reduction and a 0–3% catch reduction. A June closure produced smaller recovery, 0–1%, but also smaller catch and profit losses. These results clarify a trade-off between short-run economic efficiency and biological rebuilding, but they should not be interpreted as a policy experiment.

#### Retail, import substitution, and price transmission

FAO market reporting provides additional Korean context. In December 2025, domestic Pacific mackerel retailed at approximately 4,690 won per fish, or US$3.15, up 16.9% year on year. Imported Atlantic mackerel cost approximately 5,180 won per fish, or US$3.50, up 28.8%. In early 2026, Korea doubled its zero-tariff import quota to 20,000 tonnes and released stockpiles at discounts of 30–50% to stabilize costs ([FAO small-pelagics analysis](https://openknowledge.fao.org/bitstreams/7ad0f7a1-8766-46d5-9cf2-1402f547b832/download)).

The same report records 144,484 tonnes of Korean Pacific-mackerel exports valued at US$260 million in 2025, up 83.4% in volume and 128.8% in value from 2024. This differs from the Busan-linked figures of 144.2 thousand tonnes and US$200 million. The two records should not be combined: they may use different commodity definitions, species inclusions, product forms, or valuation rules. The discrepancy is itself evidence that trade statistics need careful reconciliation before they are used in biological-market models.

A Korean nonlinear autoregressive distributed lag study found that import prices significantly affected retail prices and identified 12 asymmetric price-transmission relationships across import, producer, wholesale, and retail stages ([Korean Journal of Fisheries and Marine Education](https://doi.org/10.47085/kjfme.40.1.4)). Price decreases and increases were transmitted differently across stages. This supports the idea that market shocks can be amplified or dampened as they move through the value chain, although the supplied result does not provide a common cross-country elasticity.

### Japan: important market, incomplete species resolution

Japan has a strong official statistical infrastructure. The e-Stat fisheries distribution survey measures monthly landing quantity and wholesale prices at major fishing ports ([e-Stat fisheries distribution survey](https://www.e-stat.go.jp/stat-search/files?toukei=00502005&tstat=000001061232)). The JAFIC archive also provides monthly and annual item-level landing, wholesale, use, and frozen-inventory tables, including generic frozen “saba” categories ([JAFIC archive](https://www.market.jafic.or.jp/file/fKoukai2025.html)).

The supplied 2025 fresh-fish table reports 47,750 kg of generic *saba* worth 25,388,601 yen, for an average unit price of 532 yen/kg. The 2024 table reports 42,329 kg worth 20,183,322 yen, for an average of 477 yen/kg ([2025 table](https://www.f-ichiba.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/R07_suisan_hinmoku.pdf); [2024 table](https://www.f-ichiba.jp/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/R06_suisan_hinmoku.pdf)). The 2025 table’s listed monthly average prices range from 424 to 691 yen/kg. However, the month columns are presented in a nonchronological order, and the category is generic *saba*, not a species-resolved *S. japonicus* series.

The Japan Fisheries Agency’s major-item origin-price table lists aggregate *saba-rui* values of 86 in 2008, 108 in 2013, 81 in 2016, 85 in 2017, and 97 in 2018. The table does not state the unit in the supplied row, and it does not resolve *S. japonicus* from *S. australasicus* ([Japan Fisheries Agency table](https://www.jfa.maff.go.jp/j/kikaku/wpaper/h30_h/trend/1/sankou_2_9.html)). These values can indicate broad category movement but cannot serve as a species-specific real-price series.

A separate frozen-mackerel benchmark lists Japan at 6.19, 6.29, 6.62, 6.38, 7.00, and 6.83 USD/kg from October 2025 through March 2026. It does not identify whether the benchmark is retail, wholesale, import, export, or processing price, and the category includes multiple *Scomber* species ([Tridge frozen-mackerel overview](https://www.tridge.com/market-overview/frozen-mackerel)). The values are therefore useful for current market context, not for direct comparison with Korean auction prices.

Japan’s import demand is substantial. FAO reports 68,996 tonnes of Asia-Pacific frozen-mackerel imports in 2025, down 13.75% from 2024. The measure is aggregate frozen mackerel, not *S. japonicus* alone. In the Tridge 2024 HS 030354 table, Japan ranked first among listed importers with 67,713,918 kg valued at US$174,495,595, while South Korea ranked fourth with 38,876,471 kg valued at US$90,241,587. Because HS 030354 differs from the HS 030374 category used elsewhere on the same page, the series must not be pooled ([Tridge trade tables](https://www.tridge.com/market-overview/frozen-mackerel)).

The Japanese market therefore supports three conclusions. Japan is a major consumer, importer, and processor; its official data can support port-level time series; and the readily supplied records do not yet provide a fully species-resolved, inflation-adjusted, cross-market price panel.

### China: major producer and processor, but aggregate price records

China’s role is substantial in both Northwest Pacific harvesting and frozen-mackerel trade. FAO reports 96,586 tonnes of Asia-Pacific frozen-mackerel imports into China in 2025, up 14.28% from 2024 ([FAO small-pelagics analysis](https://openknowledge.fao.org/bitstreams/7ad0f7a1-8766-46d5-9cf2-1402f547b832/download)). Tridge’s visible supplier-linked frozen-mackerel series reports China at 1.39, 1.28, 1.20, 1.30, 1.33, and 2.19 USD/kg from October 2025 through March 2026.

Those values are not a chub-mackerel price series. They cover frozen mackerel transactions with unspecified species, products, grades, and market levels. One sampled transaction labeled frozen chub mackerel from China to South Korea was 0.75 USD/kg on 12 February 2026, while a China-to-Canada transaction was 7.88 USD/kg on 11 February 2026. The product labels were masked, so these are route-specific examples, not evidence of a standardized price difference.

Chinese market databases identify national monthly aquatic-product wholesale series and daily or weekly regional price indices, but the supplied pages do not expose chub-mackerel observations, units, dates, or product definitions ([Hibor index](http://pur.hibor.com.cn/edbweb/edb/0201010A/2.html); [Huibo EDB](http://bw.fygsoft.com/edbweb/edb/0201010A01/1.html)). The available Chinese producer-price index for sea fish and shellfish is an aggregate quarterly index ending in 2010 and cannot identify *S. japonicus*.

China’s biological and fishery records are more informative than its supplied prices. China’s high-seas purse-seine logbooks distinguish *S. japonicus* and *S. australasicus* through field identification and model-based separation. Chub mackerel occupies a broader 35–47.5°N range than blue mackerel, whose high-abundance area is concentrated around 35–44°N and 145–160°E. SST was the strongest species differentiator, with chlorophyll-a and northward velocity further separating habitat use ([Zhang et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/ani15192822)). This demonstrates why Chinese mixed-catch price and quantity records should not be treated as taxonomically resolved without additional identification.

### Russia: important fishery, wrong species in many market indicators

Russia resumed Northwest Pacific mackerel fishing in 2015. In 2021 its fleet caught approximately 87,000 tonnes of chub mackerel, and the NPFC’s 2026 fishery summary reports that Russian mackerel catch has been approximately 100% *S. japonicus* since 2014. More than 90% of Russian mackerel catch is taken by mid-water trawlers, with smaller purse-seine and bottom-trawl components ([NPFC 2026 summary](https://www.npfc.int/system/files/2026-01/Chub%20Mackerel%202026.pdf)).

Russian domestic market reports, however, frequently label the product as Atlantic mackerel rather than *S. japonicus*. On 23 September 2024, the Central-region wholesale price for Atlantic mackerel was 237 RUB/kg and the retail price for frozen unprocessed Atlantic mackerel was 235 RUB/kg. On 3 August 2020, generic or Atlantic mackerel was reported at 130 RUB/kg wholesale and 133 RUB/kg retail, with prices declining during that week ([Russian market report, 2024](https://www.nfr.ru/media/files/monitoring/2024/monitoring.rinka.ribi.na.23.09.2024.pdf); [Russian market report, 2020](https://www.nfr.ru/media/files/monitoring/2020/monitoring.03.08.2020.pdf)).

These two observations illustrate weekly market shocks and the difference between a price episode and a price trend. They cannot be assigned to Northwest Pacific chub mackerel. Tridge’s visible frozen-mackerel series reports Russia at 2.42–2.99 USD/kg during October 2025–March 2026, but again does not identify species or market level.

Russia is therefore highly relevant to Northwest Pacific supply and catch, but the supplied market evidence cannot connect Russian chub-mackerel biology to a species-specific domestic price series.

### The United States and Mexico: a distinct eastern-Pacific case

The U.S.–Mexico stock is not interchangeable with the Northwest Pacific stocks. The 2023 U.S. assessment reports total regional landings of 32,060 tonnes in 2020, 10,416 tonnes in 2021, and 16,000 tonnes in 2022. Mexico accounted for 31,368 tonnes and the United States for 691 tonnes in 2020 ([NOAA/PFMC assessment](https://www.pcouncil.org/documents/2023/06/assessment-of-pacific-mackerel-scomber-japonicus-for-u-s-management-in-the-2023-24-and-2024-25-fishing-years.pdf/)).

The assessment provides biomass, exploitation, and management quantities but not comparable market prices. The stock is managed with an 18,200-tonne biomass cutoff, a 30% exploitation fraction, and a 70% assumed U.S.-water distribution. Mexico’s harvest was not quota-regulated in the assessment period. These policy differences mean that an observed landing-price movement could reflect management access, fleet behavior, or cross-border allocation rather than only stock abundance.

PacFIN is a useful source of U.S. landed prices and revenue. Its report defines landed weight in metric tonnes, revenue in U.S. dollars, and price in dollars per pound. However, the accessible detailed reports supplied here were run on 15 September 2026, two days after the evidence cutoff. They show 1,565.76 tonnes and US$908,452 at US$0.26/lb for the 2024–2025 season, and 1,493.99 tonnes and US$891,282 at US$0.27/lb for 2025–2026. Because the reports postdate the requested cutoff, these figures are supplemental rather than cutoff-bounded findings ([PacFIN CPS002](https://apex.psmfc.org/pacfin/f?p=501%3A302%3A9621825401282%3AINITIAL%3A%3A%3A%3A)).

PacFIN also reports confidentiality suppression, provisional status, and exclusion of Canadian and Alaskan catches. Its landed price is not a retail or wholesale price and is not adjusted for inflation, fish size, condition, or product form. A complete U.S.–Mexico market comparison therefore remains unavailable.

### Chile and Peru: context rather than pooled chub-mackerel markets

Chile’s 2020 production statistics distinguish 86,045 tonnes of Pacific chub mackerel from 556,494 tonnes of Chilean jack mackerel. Chile’s fish-product exports totaled US$5.94 billion in 2020, but the trade aggregates were 61% processed and 39% unprocessed on the export side and are not chub-specific ([FAO GLOBEFISH Chile profile](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/1429d540-6834-4b32-8ced-1eeb852b5119/content)). SERNAPESCA provides species-, month-, region-, port-, gear-, and processing-resolved landing tables, but the supplied index contains no chub-mackerel price observations ([SERNAPESCA statistical yearbooks](https://www.sernapesca.cl/informacion-utilidad/anuarios-estadisticos-de-pesca-y-acuicultura/)).

A Tridge page reports one Chile-to-Colombia frozen chub-mackerel fillet transaction at 3.17 USD/kg on 28 October 2025. It is the only transaction in that page’s sample and cannot establish a monthly or annual price pattern ([Tridge Chile fillet page](https://www.tridge.com/market-overview/frozen-chub-mackerel-fillet/CL)).

Peruvian reports describe *S. japonicus* as part of the Humboldt-system fishery but provide detailed size, abundance, and environmental information mainly for *T. murphyi*. Their jack-mackerel landings changed with oceanographic distribution, coastal-trapped Kelvin waves, Ekman transport, and fishing-season substitution. Those are valuable examples of environment–fishery interaction but cannot be converted into a chub-mackerel price series.

### Cross-market benchmark evidence

The visible Tridge frozen-mackerel series offers a common currency and frequency, but not common taxonomy or market level. The following table should therefore be read as a benchmark of supplier-linked frozen-mackerel transactions, not a comparison of *S. japonicus* prices.

| Country | Visible monthly unit-price range, Oct 2025–Mar 2026 | Pattern in visible months | Taxonomic and market qualification |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Japan | 6.19–7.00 USD/kg | Generally high and fairly stable | Frozen mackerel category; level and species unresolved |
| South Korea | 4.77–6.51 USD/kg | Increase after December | Frozen mackerel category; not equivalent to Busan auction |
| China | 1.20–2.19 USD/kg | Low through February, sharp March increase | Aggregate frozen mackerel; species and route mix unresolved |
| Russia | 2.42–2.99 USD/kg | Moderate variation | Aggregate frozen mackerel; not necessarily *S. japonicus* |
| Chile | 1.51–2.44 USD/kg | More variable | Aggregate frozen mackerel; product mix unresolved |
| Mexico | 0.90–3.30 USD/kg | Highly variable, with low volume in some months | Aggregate frozen mackerel; sample selection likely important |
| Taiwan | 2.29–2.38 USD/kg | Narrow visible range | Aggregate frozen mackerel; supplier-linked transactions |

The page summarizes 23,064 supplier-linked transactions across 20 countries, but it is not a census of all transactions. The later six months of 2026 are hidden, and the page does not define a uniform retail, wholesale, auction, or processing level ([Tridge frozen-mackerel overview](https://www.tridge.com/market-overview/frozen-mackerel)). The table can identify broad price dispersion and possible trade-route differences; it cannot establish that Japanese chub mackerel is more valuable than Chinese or Mexican chub mackerel.

## Interannual variation in weight and length

### Why size comparisons are difficult

Length and weight are not one measurement. Studies use fork length (FL), total length (TL), or standard length (SL), and these cannot be converted across stocks without a stock- and species-specific relationship. Weight depends on length, sex, maturity, feeding history, lipid reserves, season, and condition.

A standard weight–length model is:

$$W=aL^b.$$

In a Northwest Pacific sample of 2,686 fish collected from Chinese vessels during 2016–2020, the fitted relationship was:

$$W=1.41\times10^{-6}FL^{3.37},$$

with weight in grams and fork length in millimetres. The exponent \(b=3.37\) indicates positive allometry: weight increased faster than the cube of fork length in that dataset ([Cai et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-1312/10/2/301)). This equation should not be applied automatically to Korean, Japanese, eastern-Pacific, Chilean, or Peruvian fish.

Age, sex, gear, area, season, and sample composition also matter. Chinese high-seas samples had a median fork length of 220 mm near Japan but only 150 mm in Zhejiang coastal waters. Autumn fish were larger and heavier than summer fish, and 2020 fish were significantly larger and heavier than those in other years. These differences could reflect geography and season rather than interannual population change.

### Northwest Pacific weight at age

The NPFC’s 2025 assessment combines catch-at-length, age–length keys, and weight-at-age for China, eastern and western Japan, and Russia. The assessment covers seven age groups: ages 0–5 and a 6+ group. Catch-at-length coverage begins in 2016 for China and Russia and in 2014 for Japan; quarterly weight-at-age coverage begins in 2018 for China, 2014 for Japan, and 2016 for Russia ([NPFC 2025 assessment](https://www.npfc.int/system/files/2026-04/Stock%20assessment%20report%20for%20chub%20mackerel%202025.pdf)).

The annual weight-at-age series for FY2014–FY2023 is a catch-number-weighted aggregation of quarterly member and regional values. For FY1970–FY2013, the assessment substitutes Japanese Pacific-stock weights because other members did not provide historical values. Consequently, the long-term series is useful for direction and stock assessment but is not a fully comparable observation series across countries.

The assessment reports that weight at age is time varying and decreased noticeably during the last decade for age groups older than age 0. A 2024 NPFC working paper likewise reports that weight at age became lighter after the 2013 year class, remained light, and showed only slight recovery for age-4-and-older fish ([NPFC base-case data description](https://www.npfc.int/system/files/2024-07/NPFC-2024-TWG%20CMSA09-WP01%20Input_data_base_case%20ppt.pdf)).

This matters because spawning stock biomass is calculated from numbers, weight, and maturity:

$$SSB_t=\sum_a N_{a,t}w_{a,t}g_{a,t}.$$

A decline in weight at age reduces estimated spawning biomass even if the number of fish is unchanged. The NPFC assessment also reports a recent decline in maturity at age, so the biological changes affect both biomass and reproductive potential.

Japan’s 2019 Pacific-coast assessment example found that weight at ages 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6+ was the lowest since 1970, while ages 0 and 1 remained low relative to other years. The supplied report gives relative rankings rather than gram values, so a year-by-year numerical weight table cannot be reconstructed from the evidence ([Manabe et al.](https://www.npfc.int/system/files/2020-10/NPFC-2020-TWG%20CMSA03-WP02%20Catch%2C%20weight%2C%20and%20maturity%20at%20age%20of%20the%20chub%20mackerel%20of%20Japan.pdf)).

### Korean landed size and grade composition

The Korean Busan study provides the most detailed annual landed-size evidence for a commercial market. Between 2014 and 2025:

- Mean fork length varied from 26.4 to 29.4 cm.
- Mean fork length changed from 28.7 to 27.9 cm, but the trend was not significant, p = 0.24.
- The proportion below the estimated 29.5 cm fork-length maturity threshold changed from 66% to 78%, also not significantly, p = 0.15.
- The below-threshold proportion ranged from 48% to 85%.
- Grades 3–4 comprised 92–100% of landed weight throughout.
- Grade 4 increased from 77% to 97% of landed weight, p = 0.003.

The key distinction is between landed size and size at age. The landing composition is shaped by fishing ground, season, gear selectivity, fleet behavior, and market sorting. The study had no ageing data and therefore could not determine whether smaller landings reflected slower growth, younger cohorts, or a change in where the fleet fished ([Yoo and Yoon](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2026.1945408/full)).

The 2025 winter relocation illustrates the problem. The Southern East Sea had a 97.0% Grade 4 share, compared with 75.3% outside the region. Within Grade 4, however, mean fork length was 28.1 cm in the Southern East Sea and 27.6 cm elsewhere. The region was therefore smaller mainly because it produced more Grade 4 fish, not because Grade 4 fish were individually smaller there.

The seasonal contrast also favors a fishery-structure explanation. Between the earliest and latest three-year windows, feeding-season mean fork length fell by 0.6 cm, while overwintering-season mean fork length fell by 1.7 cm. Neither seasonal trend was significant, so this is supporting evidence rather than proof. A population-wide decline in size at age remains possible.

### High-seas length-frequency and LBB results

A 2019–2024 high-seas study sampled 6,061 *S. japonicus* from 38–46°N and 147–162°E. Monthly light-purse-seine sampling from April to December collected at least 25 fish per station, with an aggregate fork-length range of 102–435 mm ([Zhang et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/fishes11050276)).

The study estimated annual asymptotic fork length, \(L_\infty\), with a length-based Bayesian biomass model. \(L_\infty\) is the theoretical length approached under the fitted growth model; it is not an observed annual mean or median.

| Year or pooled period | \(L_\infty\) (cm) | \(L_c/L_{c-opt}\) | \(B/B_0\) | \(B/B_{MSY}\) | Status |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 2019 | 43.7 | 0.77 | 0.45 | 1.20 | Healthy |
| 2020 | 46.0 | 0.76 | 0.21 | 0.57 | Overfished |
| 2021 | 40.3 | 0.60 | 0.80 | 2.10 | Healthy |
| 2022 | 39.4 | 0.75 | 0.67 | 1.80 | Healthy |
| 2023 | 45.3 | 0.77 | 0.09 | 0.24 | Severely overfished |
| 2024 | 41.2 | 0.84 | 0.22 | 0.59 | Overfished |
| 2019–2020 | 44.5 | 0.77 | 0.35 | 1.02 | Healthy |
| 2021–2022 | 44.9 | 0.83 | 0.45 | 1.30 | Healthy |
| 2023–2024 | 43.6 | 0.80 | 0.19 | 0.51 | Overfished |

The annual \(L_\infty\) values fluctuated from 39.4 cm in 2022 to 46.0 cm in 2020 and rose to 41.2 cm in 2024. The study found no clear long-term trend in growth potential. Annual stock-status reversals were much sharper than would normally be expected from true population change alone; the authors attribute them partly to single-year sampling error, environmental perturbation, and stochastic noise.

Pooling adjacent years produced a more coherent result: 2019–2020 and 2021–2022 were assessed as healthy, while 2023–2024 had \(B/B_{MSY}=0.51\). The pooled estimate is more stable than any single-year value but still depends on the LBB model’s assumptions about selectivity, asymptotic length, mortality, and length-frequency representativeness.

The LBB results therefore support recent biological stress, but they do not provide a direct series of observed annual mean weight or length. They are model-based proxies for fishing pressure and biomass status.

### Japanese sampling and age composition

Japan has the most extensive biological sampling system among the Northwest Pacific members. Its Pacific-coast assessment collects catch data from 19 prefectures and approximately 60,000 individual length records annually. Fork length is measured to 1 mm, weight to 0.1 g, and a prefecture-year relationship converts length to weight. Age–length keys are built separately for northeastern and southwestern groups and for four seasonal quarters ([Manabe et al.](https://www.npfc.int/system/files/2020-10/NPFC-2020-TWG%20CMSA03-WP02%20Catch%2C%20weight%2C%20and%20maturity%20at%20age%20of%20the%20chub%20mackerel%20of%20Japan.pdf)).

In 2019, the Japanese sample contained 65,122 fork-length measurements, 13,728 individual weights, and 3,915 aged fish. The northeastern group contributed 42,974 lengths and 2,207 ages; the southwestern group contributed 22,148 lengths and 1,708 ages. These sample sizes are large, but they do not automatically produce a single comparable annual mean because the stock migrates seasonally and the sample is stratified by region, gear, month, and port.

Some Japanese prefectures combine *S. japonicus* and *S. australasicus* as “mackerels” and estimate the *S. japonicus* share from monthly subsamples. That procedure is useful for assessment but reinforces the need to preserve species-coding metadata when comparing markets.

### Northeastern Pacific size and age evidence

The eastern North Pacific provides a separate biological case. SWFSC acoustic-trawl surveys from 2012–2022 sampled fish from Vancouver Island to Baja California ranging from 53 to 402 mm fork length. Among 1,762 aged fish, ages 0, 1, 2, and 3 represented 46%, 29%, 16%, and 6%, while ages 4–7 comprised only 2.3%. CDFW fishery-dependent port samples from 2008–2022 ranged from 84 to 429 mm FL and included 9,035 aged fish from ages 0–9; ages 4–9 represented only 4% ([NOAA life-history report](https://repository.library.noaa.gov/view/noaa/52097/noaa_52097_DS1.pdf)).

The age distributions show why survey and landing composition must be kept separate. Fishery-dependent port samples and fishery-independent acoustic-trawl samples are subject to different selectivity, locations, and seasonal coverage. The assessment estimates female length at 50% maturity at 274 ± 1.26 mm FL and age at 50% maturity at 1.01 ± 0.06 years, but does not provide a complete annual individual-level weight and length series.

Age-reading uncertainty is also material. Agreement between two readers was 100% at ages 0–2, 94% at age 3, 75% at age 4, and 70% at age 5. There is no age-validation study for the eastern North Pacific stock. Thus, even where age data exist, uncertainty is not uniform across age groups.

### Condition, lipid content, and body quality

Biological quality is multidimensional. In Korean coastal samples, total length and body weight were strongly associated with crude lipid content from July through December: length–lipid \(r^2\) ranged from 0.71 to 0.83, while weight–lipid \(r^2\) ranged from 0.78 to 0.87 ([Shim et al.](https://www.trjfas.org/pdf.php?id=1043)). Adult fish longer than 35 cm had high lipid content and were considered in the best nutritional condition, coinciding with maturation. Fat content declined through winter as feeding weakened and stored energy was used.

In the Pacific stock off northeastern Japan, 2,085 purse-seine fish measuring 21–42 cm FL were sampled during 2012–2017. Crude fat content and condition factor were high from September to January and declined slightly in February; March–August samples were small, limiting seasonal comparison ([Japanese Fisheries Oceanography study](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jsfo/83/1/83_19/_article/-char/en)). A generalized additive model found significant year effects, including positive effects on crude fat in 2016 and 2017, but the supplied abstract does not give effect sizes or identify the causes.

A comparison of La Niña 2021 and El Niño 2023 samples found that 100–200 mm fish had significantly higher Fulton’s condition factor during El Niño, whereas fish above 250 mm had reduced condition. Female–male differences in condition present in 2021 disappeared in 2023. Trophic niche breadth expanded from 4.12 to 6.88 standardized ellipse area units, suggesting dietary diversification ([Zhao et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40318477/)). The comparison covers one year of each climate state, so it indicates a possible mechanism rather than a general ENSO law.

## Oceanographic theory and biological mechanisms

### The physical setting

The Northwest Pacific is shaped by the interaction of the Tsushima, Kuroshio, Kuroshio Extension, and Oyashio currents. These create fronts, transition zones, strong gradients in temperature and salinity, variable mixed-layer depths, and areas of enhanced productivity. The East China Sea and Yellow Sea have high productivity because of shallow-seafloor nutrient supply and river discharge. The open Kuroshio region is less productive because strong stratification limits nutrient mixing, while the Oyashio and Kuroshio–Oyashio Transition Zone support strong seasonal production ([Yatsu review](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3)).

The biological pathway is seasonal. Spawning occurs in subtropical waters around the Kuroshio and its extension, where copepod nauplii are available to larvae. Currents transport eggs and larvae toward nursery and feeding regions. During summer and autumn, adult and juvenile fish use the Oyashio, northern Japan Sea, Yellow Sea, East China Sea, and transition zones where larger zooplankton such as *Euphausia pacifica*, *Neocalanus*, and *Calanus sinicus* are available.

This physical setting links distribution to oceanography in a direct way, but not in a simple one-to-one way. A current may transport larvae into a productive nursery in one year and away from it in another. Temperature can accelerate growth within a suitable range, but extreme heat can reduce prey, increase metabolic costs, or displace fish.

### Temperature, currents, fronts, and larval transport

The von Bertalanffy growth function used in length-based studies expresses length as an asymptotic approach:

$$L_t=L_\infty[1-e^{-K(t-t_0)}].$$

Environmental conditions influence both the observed growth coefficient \(K\) and the probability that a cohort survives to recruitment.

Otolith back-calculation from 532 larvae and juveniles collected in the Kuroshio–Oyashio transition region during 2002–2011 found April-cohort daily growth rates ranging from 1.03 ± 0.10 mm/day in 2006 to 1.52 ± 0.23 mm/day in 2009. Daily growth and larval-stage duration were significantly related to recruitment estimates, and fish-specific experienced SST was significantly related to growth ([Kamimura et al.](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12562-015-0869-4)). Higher temperature within the suitable range produced faster growth and a shorter larval stage.

The mechanism is important because faster early growth can reduce the time larvae are exposed to predation and starvation. But this does not mean that warmer water is always beneficial. The relevant relationship is nonlinear: temperature must be considered together with prey, transport, oxygen, and the species’ thermal niche.

The Kuroshio path also matters. Studies of the Pacific stock associate high recruitment with combinations of winter conditions favorable to adults around the Izu Islands and spring conditions that efficiently transport eggs and larvae toward suitable nursery waters. A Type-N Kuroshio path can produce different conditions from a Type-C path, and the relative importance of these pathways changes across ocean regimes ([Yatsu review](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3)).

### Chlorophyll-a, productivity, and prey

Chlorophyll-a is a proxy for phytoplankton biomass and lower-trophic production, not a direct measure of fish food. It becomes biologically meaningful when translated through zooplankton, prey encounter rates, and larval feeding.

A full-life-cycle bioenergetics and population-dynamics model for 1998–2018 separated SST and chlorophyll-a forcing. The model found that chlorophyll-a was the principal driver of stock fluctuations overall, strongly influenced the increase during 2010–2014, and that SST became more influential after 2014. The model converted chlorophyll-a into prey conditions and then into daily growth, survival, recruitment, and biomass ([bioenergetics model](https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2023.1142899)).

The model is mechanistically useful but not a causal observation. It uses fixed migration routes and simulated environmental experiments. Its result should be interpreted as evidence that productivity and temperature are plausible pathways through which the environment affects stock dynamics, not as a measured chlorophyll-to-price coefficient.

Larval surveys in southern Japan also support a prey mechanism. In 2018 and 2019, copepods and appendicularians were found in *S. japonicus* larval diets. Appendicularian occurrence increased among larger larvae, but the size effect was not statistically significant. Larval density had a weak negative association with chlorophyll-a, \(r^2=0.065\), p < 0.05, indicating that chlorophyll alone is not a sufficient biological explanation ([Kume et al.](https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2021.725227)).

### PDO, NPGO, ENSO, and other climate variability

The Pacific Decadal Oscillation and North Pacific Gyre Oscillation affect the position and strength of the Kuroshio–Oyashio Extension. A review describes a two- to three-year lag between PDO/NPGO-related Rossby waves and circulation changes. Positive phases shift and intensify the Kuroshio–Oyashio Extension southward ([Yatsu review](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3)).

An NPFC analysis of Japan’s 1995–2022 catch series found a contemporaneous correlation of 0.60 between a two-year low-pass PDO and chub-mackerel catch, and 0.56 when PDO led catch by one year; both had p = 0.0005. The same analysis found no relationship between the Oyashio southern-limit index and catch, \(r=-0.01\), p = 0.74 ([NPFC environmental analysis](https://www.npfc.int/system/files/2024-07/NPFC-2024-TWG%20CMSA09-IP01%20NPFC_CM_Decrease_2024.pdf)).

These two findings should be considered together. PDO may summarize a broad regime that influences several environmental processes, while the Oyashio index may be too coarse, too localized, or mismatched in timing to capture the relevant mechanism. The null Oyashio result does not disprove oceanographic influence; it limits the claim that this particular index directly explains Japanese catch variation during 1995–2022.

A broader stock comparison found that regional temperature-suitability indices predicted Pacific-stock biomass and recruitment with one- and two-year lags, but explained Tsushima Current catch and recruitment poorly. Chinese catch was negatively associated with some temperature-suitability indices while Japanese and Korean Tsushima catch was positively associated. Chinese catch also depended on total fishing-boat engine power, showing that fishing effort confounded the environmental relationship ([stock-comparison study](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2022.996626/full)).

ENSO effects are similarly stock- and species-specific. A habitat-model comparison of *S. japonicus* and Japanese sardine used SST, sea-surface height, and chlorophyll-a under different ENSO conditions. The suitable-habitat area for *S. japonicus* was reported as less than 6%, while sardine exceeded 15%; the *S. japonicus* habitat-area growth rate was 1.114 under La Niña and 2.082 under El Niño. The units and uncertainty of those growth rates were not supplied, so they should be treated as model outputs rather than general effect sizes ([ENSO habitat study](https://castjournals.cast.org.cn/joweb/hyxb/EN/1200024644913820142)).

### Marine heatwaves

Marine heatwaves are defined in the supplied study as events in which SST exceeds a seasonally varying 90th-percentile threshold for at least five consecutive days, with events separated by two days or less merged. Using Chinese logbook CPUE from 2014–2021 and NOAA OISST data, the study found increasing heatwave frequency, intensity, and duration alongside declining CPUE.

The reported frequency–CPUE correlation was −0.72, p < 0.001. A generalized additive model found a nonlinear intensity effect, with effective degrees of freedom 6.49, F = 15.74, and adjusted \(R^2=0.336\), explaining 33.9% of deviance after including duration, year, month, longitude, and latitude ([Ji et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/fishes11010013)). CPUE was lower during heatwaves than non-heatwave periods, and often rebounded afterward, although not always to pre-event levels.

This is strong association evidence but not causal identification. The study uses CPUE as an abundance indicator, yet CPUE also changes with fleet location, catchability, effort, and fish aggregation. The authors also note that the model does not include salinity, currents, or prey. A heatwave can reduce catch because fish die, move, move vertically, disperse, or become harder to catch. Those mechanisms have different implications for stock biomass and market supply.

### Environmental lags

The evidence implies at least four distinct time scales:

| Process | Approximate response time | Biological or market meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Heatwave-driven movement or CPUE change | Days to months | Immediate availability and fishing efficiency |
| Seasonal lipid and condition change | Months | Freshness, nutritional value, spawning allocation |
| Larval growth and recruitment | One to two years | Cohort strength and later catchable biomass |
| PDO/NPGO circulation effects | Two to three years | Delayed changes in transport, productivity, and recruitment |

A price series sampled monthly can therefore respond to a biological event that occurred years earlier, a contemporaneous fishing-ground shift, a quota decision, or an unrelated trade shock. Correlating annual prices with annual SST without matching these lags would be biologically and economically ambiguous.

## Biological quality, fishery economics, and market transmission

### Quality is more than size

Commercial quality has at least four dimensions:

- Size and grade, which determine product channel and consumer use.
- Condition and lipid content, which affect taste, texture, energy value, and maturation.
- Freshness and time–temperature history, which affect sensory quality and histamine risk.
- Processing and cold-chain condition, including bruising, belly burst, oxidation, dehydration, freezer burn, glaze, and packaging.

Frozen-mackerel specifications identify size band, whole-fish integrity, glaze, freezer burn, oxidation odor, and documented time–temperature control as grading factors ([Tridge quality specification](https://www.tridge.com/market-overview/frozen-mackerel)). Because mackerel is oily, oxidation and freezer burn can reduce sensory quality, increase trim loss, and raise claim risk during long-haul trade. Histamine risk is controlled through rapid chilling, freezing, and stable cold-chain management.

The available evidence does not provide a species-specific price elasticity for lipid, freshness, oxidation, or cold-chain quality. It supports the mechanism qualitatively, but not a numerical quality-price function.

### Supply: biomass, recruitment, catch, and effort

Supply is not simply landings. It reflects stock biomass, recruitment, fish distribution, fleet capacity, catchability, quotas, fishing costs, weather, processing capacity, inventories, and trade demand.

The NPFC 2025 assessment estimates that total chub-mackerel catch in the Convention Area declined from roughly 516 thousand tonnes in 2018 to 129 thousand tonnes in 2024. The 2025 fishing-season Convention Area limit was 66,740 tonnes. The assessment also reports declining spawning stock biomass, lower maturity at age, lower weight at age, and current fishing mortality above several biological reference points ([NPFC 2025 assessment](https://www.npfc.int/system/files/2026-04/Stock%20assessment%20report%20for%20chub%20mackerel%202025.pdf)).

The historical transition is important:

- The stock was abundant in the 1970s.
- Biomass declined through the 1980s and remained low through the 1990s and early 2000s.
- Overfishing and high fishing capacity contributed to delayed recovery.
- Reduced exploitation and strong year classes supported recovery after the mid-2000s.
- A strong 2013 year class contributed to rapid improvement in the 2010s.
- Biomass peaked around FY2018 in the NPFC assessment and then declined sharply.

The Japanese small-pelagic-fish review identifies a capacity–productivity mismatch as a central historical mechanism. Large purse-seine investment during the 1980s was followed by the 1988/89 environmental regime shift and lower productivity. Fishing capacity persisted after ecological conditions deteriorated, contributing to overfishing in the 1990s and early 2000s ([Yatsu review](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3)).

This history shows why catch alone cannot identify environmental effects. Commercial catch is a function of biomass, fishing mortality, catchability, and effort. Changes in gear, fleet size, search technology, and fishing location can increase or decrease landings independently of biomass.

### Size composition and market transmission

A change in biological size composition can affect markets in three ways.

First, it changes the quantity of fish entering each commercial grade. A cohort dominated by small fish may increase volume in export, canning, or feed channels while reducing domestic food-grade supply.

Second, it changes the average value per kilogram. This can reduce total revenue even when tonnes remain constant, unless a new market absorbs the lower grade.

Third, it can change fishing behavior. If the small-fish channel becomes profitable, vessels may relocate toward nursery-adjacent grounds or alter timing and gear use. This is the mechanism suggested by the Korean 2025 case.

The Korean data show that Grade 4 remained a low-price product relative to Grade 1, but the export outlet made large volumes economically viable. The market did not reward small fish with a premium; it changed the feasible scale of their sale.

### Trade shocks and substitution

FAO reports that Atlantic mackerel quota reductions lowered global Atlantic supply and raised prices. In 2025 the Atlantic catch quota was down 22% year on year, and the 2026–2028 overall quota was reported at 299,010 tonnes, 48% below the 2025 figure. Importers and processors increasingly considered Pacific chub and Chilean jack mackerel as alternatives ([FAO small-pelagics analysis](https://openknowledge.fao.org/bitstreams/7ad0f7a1-8766-46d5-9cf2-1402f547b832/download)).

This is a substitution mechanism, not evidence that Pacific chub prices are determined by its own biomass alone. An Atlantic supply shock can raise demand for Pacific chub even when Pacific biological conditions are unchanged. Conversely, a Pacific stock decline can raise Pacific prices if substitution options are limited.

The Asia-Pacific frozen-mackerel import total rose from 654,254 tonnes in 2024 to 712,384 tonnes in 2025, an 8.87% increase. China’s imports rose 14.28%, Korea’s 36.58%, while Japan’s declined 13.75%. These are aggregate frozen-mackerel quantities and include multiple species and product forms, but they demonstrate that regional demand can move differently across countries.

Prepared or preserved mackerel imports under HS 160415 rose from 152,980 tonnes in 2024 to 160,974 tonnes in 2025, a 4.57% increase. This processed-product series is distinct from whole-frozen, wholesale, retail, and landing measures. It shows how processing can buffer or redirect raw-fish supply rather than simply passing through landing prices.

### Costs, quotas, and processing margins

Observed fishing-cost and processing-cost series are not populated in the supplied evidence. The Korean optimal-harvest model assumes a constant effort cost and explores sensitivity to changing cost levels. It finds that higher costs reduce effort, catch, and profit while increasing biomass, but this is a simulation rather than an observed cost response ([Jang and Cho](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13662-025-03898-9)).

Similarly, the supplied sources do not provide comparable processing margins, fuel costs, cold-storage costs, inventory costs, or vessel-specific profitability across countries. This prevents a fully integrated supply–quality–price model.

Quota effects are nevertheless visible. Japan reduced Pacific-stock quota levels, and NPFC measures impose Convention Area limits, gear sublimits, vessel restrictions, and monthly electronic reporting ([NPFC 2026 summary](https://www.npfc.int/system/files/2026-01/Chub%20Mackerel%202026.pdf)). In the United States, the management rule uses biomass thresholds and an exploitation fraction. In Korea, domestic supply and export demand interact with import quotas and stockpile releases.

These policy instruments can create price movements that resemble biological signals. A quota cut can raise price while stock biomass remains unchanged; a stockpile release can lower retail price without changing landings; and an import tariff change can alter domestic prices independently of local recruitment.

## Integrated correlations and Pacific Rim comparison

### Evidence for individual links

The available evidence supports several separate links but not one integrated causal model.

| Link | Observation or estimate | Lag and controls | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Catch to Korean price | Monthly nonlinear models \(R^2=0.724\)–0.769 | July 2017–June 2022; demand assumed stable | Catch-dependent pricing is plausible within Korea, but not a causal elasticity |
| Import to Korean retail | Significant import-price effect; 12 asymmetric transmission phenomena | NARDL across distribution stages | Market transmission is nonlinear and stage-specific |
| Grade 4 revenue to export value | Raw ρ = 0.69; detrended ρ = 0.29; differences ρ = −0.04 | 2014–2025; annual convention mismatch | Long-run co-trending, not year-to-year causal coupling |
| PDO to Japanese catch | \(r=0.60\) contemporaneous; \(r=0.56\) with one-year lead | 1995–2022; AR(1) null simulations for spatial correlations | Climate regime association with a plausible lag |
| TSI to biomass and recruitment | Significant one- and two-year lagged relationships for Pacific stock | Gradient forest, GAM, and TGAM | Stock-specific environment–biology association |
| MHW to Chinese CPUE | \(r=-0.72\), p < 0.001; GAM adjusted \(R^2=0.336\) | 2014–2021; year, month, location, duration included | Strong association, but CPUE and catchability remain confounded |
| SST to Korean fishing-ground share | ρ = 0.16, p = 0.46; ρ = 0.05 excluding 2025 | 1982/83–2024/25 SST, winter share 2001–2025 | Warming permitted access but did not explain the 2025 relocation |
| Length to lipid | Korean \(r^2=0.71\)–0.87 depending on metric | Seasonal July–December data | Size and condition co-vary, but price effect is unestimated |

The missing link is direct environment-to-market estimation. No supplied study jointly estimates price as a function of SST, currents, chlorophyll, recruitment, size, condition, effort, quota, trade, and processing while controlling for market shocks. It would be incorrect to infer such a coefficient from the separate associations.

### Correlation versus causation

Three problems recur.

#### Common trends

The Korean Grade 4 revenue-export relationship is the clearest example. Both series rose over time, producing a raw correlation. Detrending and first differencing largely removed the relationship. The same issue applies to warming and prices: a long-term temperature trend and a long-term price trend can produce correlation even if temperature did not cause the price change.

#### Catchability and spatial selection

CPUE and landed size are not direct biomass or population-size measures. Fish may move, aggregate, disperse, or become vertically inaccessible. A fleet may relocate toward a high-density nursery ground because of fish availability, market demand, fuel cost, or all three. The Korean study’s evidence is unusually strong because it links grade composition to fishing blocks, but it still cannot separate fleet choice from fish availability.

#### Policy and market shocks

Quotas, import tariffs, stockpiles, exchange rates, export demand, fuel costs, sanctions, and cold-storage inventories can all change prices or landings. A biological interpretation that omits these variables will overstate environment–market causation.

### Cross-country comparison

#### Japan and South Korea

Japan and South Korea are major consumers and processors, but their market records differ. Japan’s official port series is broader and often uses generic *saba* categories. Korea offers species-linked grades, prices, export channels, and fishing-ground data. Korea’s Tsushima Current stock is biologically closer to the Japanese western and Korean fishery than to Japan’s Pacific stock, but the fleets sample different seasons and ages.

Korean catch composition is dominated by younger fish in recent years, while Japanese Pacific-stock assessment records include extensive age-structured sampling and long historical weight-at-age data. Directly comparing mean lengths without matching stock, season, gear, and age composition would be misleading.

#### China, Japan, and Russia

The NPFC assessment integrates these members into one Pacific-stock model, but their fisheries select different ages and sizes. Chinese catches mainly comprise ages 0–2, while recent Japanese and Russian catches comprise more age-3-and-older fish ([NPFC base-case data description](https://www.npfc.int/system/files/2024-07/NPFC-2024-TWG%20CMSA09-WP01%20Input_data_base_case%20ppt.pdf)). China uses light purse seines and pelagic trawls; Japan uses purse seines, set nets, dip nets, and stick-held dip nets; Russia uses predominantly mid-water trawls.

This means a country-level average length may measure fleet selectivity rather than stock-wide size structure. It also means that a country-level price may reflect a different age and product composition.

#### United States and Mexico

The northeastern Pacific stock is managed as a transboundary unit, but Mexico supplies most reported landings in the assessment period. U.S. price records are landed prices and often provisional, while Mexican price evidence is not populated. The stock’s management boundary and assumed U.S. distribution fraction are not equivalent to biological stock boundaries.

#### Chile and Peru

Chile and Peru are important Pacific fisheries countries, but their dominant mackerel market is jack mackerel, *Trachurus murphyi*. *S. japonicus* should be retained as a separate minor or contextual category. Pooling Chilean jack-mackerel prices with Pacific chub-mackerel prices would produce a taxonomic error rather than a broader comparison.

### Conflicting stock assessments and what they mean for markets

Stock status is not settled across methods. Five state-space surplus-production models applied to the Northwest Pacific Pacific stock produced 2020 ratios ranging from slight overfishing to healthy status. CMSY, BSM, and JABBA-Select indicated possible slight overfishing, while SPiCT and JABBA indicated a healthy stock ([Cai et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/fishes8020080)).

East China Sea assessments similarly diverged, with one study estimating \(B/B_{MSY}=0.091\) and classifying the stock as collapsed, while another estimated 1.13 and classified it as healthy ([assessment comparison](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2026.1814806/full)).

The 2026 LBB study found annual reversals between healthy and overfished status, while its pooled 2023–2024 estimate was \(B/B_{MSY}=0.51\). Its Catch-MSY estimate of MSY was 278,000 tonnes, with a 95% interval of 162,000–475,000 tonnes. An earlier Catch-MSY analysis using data through 2019 estimated 496,200 tonnes, with a 95% interval of 387,200–605,200 tonnes ([LBB and Catch-MSY study](https://doi.org/10.3390/fishes11050276)).

These disagreements affect market interpretation. If the biological supply baseline is uncertain, a price increase cannot be translated confidently into a specific biomass decline or fishing-mortality estimate. The appropriate response is to combine assessment models, preserve uncertainty intervals, and avoid treating one MSY estimate as an observed economic capacity.

### A defensible integrated pathway

The evidence supports the following conditional chain:

1. Climate and oceanography alter SST, circulation, fronts, mixed-layer depth, chlorophyll, prey, and transport.
2. These conditions affect larval growth, survival, recruitment, migration, body condition, lipid content, and size at age.
3. Biological changes alter biomass, catchability, catch composition, and the quantity of fish entering each commercial grade.
4. Landings, quotas, effort, fuel cost, exchange rates, inventories, trade demand, and processing capacity determine available market supply.
5. Supply and grade composition affect auction, wholesale, import, export, and retail prices.
6. Prices and market outlets feed back into vessel location, fishing timing, target choice, and the age and size composition of future catches.

Every arrow is biologically or economically plausible. Only some arrows are quantitatively supported for particular stocks and periods. The full chain remains an evidence-based synthesis, not a demonstrated single causal model.

## Evidence limits, synthesis, and implications

### Consolidated country and market comparison

| Country or case | Biological coverage | Price coverage | Product and market level | Comparability judgment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Japan | Long catch and length sampling; Pacific and Tsushima stock usages; species sometimes aggregated | Port and wholesale records; generic *saba*; frozen-mackerel benchmarks | Fresh landing/wholesale, frozen trade, aggregate origin prices | Strong national infrastructure, but species and stock resolution incomplete |
| South Korea | Tsushima Current stock; grade, FL, weight, catch block, and condition data | Best evidence: Busan auction 2014–2025, monthly catch-price models, retail and export context | Auction, producer, wholesale, retail, export | Strongest integrated case, though exports combine mackerel species |
| China | High-seas logbooks, CPUE, species-separation models, NPFC catch | Frozen-mackerel transaction benchmarks and aggregate aquatic-price indices | Supplier-linked frozen trade; wholesale candidates not exposed | Important market and fishery, but no comparable species-specific price panel |
| Russia | NPFC *S. japonicus* catch and gear data | Domestic reports mainly Atlantic mackerel; aggregate frozen benchmarks | Wholesale, retail, export indicators | Fishery is relevant, supplied prices are not taxonomically aligned |
| United States–Mexico | Transboundary *S. japonicus* assessment, length and age surveys | U.S. landed prices available but supplied detailed reports postdate cutoff; Mexican price series unavailable | Ex-vessel/landed U.S. data; no matched Mexican series | Separate eastern-Pacific case; no cross-country price panel |
| Chile | Species-resolved production and processing statistics | One chub-mackerel fillet transaction; no time series | Production and trade context; mostly jack mackerel market | Do not pool with Northwest Pacific prices |
| Peru | *S. japonicus* present; detailed evidence dominated by *T. murphyi* | No usable chub-mackerel price series | Jack-mackerel fishery and environmental reports | Context only; taxonomic separation essential |

### Principal evidence gaps

The most consequential gaps are not simply missing numbers. They are missing definitions.

1. Customs and frozen-mackerel categories often do not distinguish *S. japonicus*, *S. australasicus*, *S. scombrus*, and *T. murphyi*.
2. Product forms and grades are not harmonized.
3. Import and export unit values use different valuation bases and may include freight, insurance, processing, or re-export effects.
4. Market levels are mixed: landing, auction, wholesale, retail, and processing prices cannot be pooled without adjustment.
5. Weight and length data use FL, TL, and SL, with different sampling designs.
6. Age, sex, cohort, gear, location, and sample-size metadata are incomplete across countries.
7. The NPFC long-term weight-at-age series substitutes Japanese values before FY2014.
8. Direct quality-price elasticities for lipid, condition, freshness, oxidation, and cold-chain history are unavailable.
9. Fishing-cost, processing-cost, inventory, and margin data are not populated across markets.
10. Direct environment-to-price and quality-to-price causal estimates are absent.
11. Stock-status estimates are sensitive to model priors, selectivity, catchability, environmental variability, and sampling.
12. The PacFIN CPS002 records run on 15 September 2026, after the 13 September cutoff, and therefore cannot support cutoff-bounded conclusions.

### Monitoring implications

A useful monitoring system should link four synchronized layers.

#### Taxonomy and product identity

National customs and landing systems should distinguish *S. japonicus* from *S. australasicus* and should identify whole round, headed and gutted, fillet, canned, and other product forms. HS codes alone are insufficient. Species verification, port sampling, and lot-level traceability are especially important when a market shock is being interpreted biologically.

#### Biological monitoring

Weight-at-age, maturity-at-age, length frequency, age composition, sex, condition factor, lipid content, and sample size should be collected together. Japan’s large annual length sample, the NPFC member surveys, Korean grade-resolved monitoring, and U.S. acoustic-trawl and port programs provide useful components, but their seasons and gears should be harmonized before cross-stock comparisons.

The Korean case shows why length at landing should be linked to fishing block and market grade. A national mean can conceal a local concentration of immature or small fish. Grade 4 share, below-maturity proportion, fishing-ground share, and distance from home port can serve as early-warning indicators when interpreted together.

#### Oceanographic monitoring

Monitoring should combine SST with currents, fronts, mixed-layer depth, chlorophyll-a, productivity, prey, oxygen, and marine heatwave metrics. A single annual temperature index is unlikely to capture the mechanisms. Recruitment models should allow one- to two-year lags, while circulation indices may require two- to three-year lags. Short-lived heatwave effects should be analyzed separately from decadal regime shifts.

#### Market monitoring

Market records should preserve the distinction between nominal and real prices and should report currency, unit, product form, grade, market level, quantity, and valuation basis. Auction and customs records should be matched through biological and inventory time rather than assuming that calendar-year landings equal calendar-year exports.

### Management implications

The biological evidence supports precaution, but the exact management response must reflect stock and market differences.

For the Northwest Pacific Pacific stock, the NPFC assessment finds declining recent biomass and weight at age and recommends reducing fishing mortality while improving biological data. The NPFC’s provisional 66,740-tonne Convention Area limit, gear sublimits, vessel restrictions, and monthly electronic reporting represent management responses to the stock’s transboundary character ([NPFC 2026 summary](https://www.npfc.int/system/files/2026-01/Chub%20Mackerel%202026.pdf)).

For Korea, a national TAC alone may not prevent concentration on small fish in a particular region and season. The 2025 evidence points toward spatial and seasonal monitoring, size-composition indicators, and market-sensitive management. A closure or size measure should be evaluated for both biological recovery and the economic displacement it creates. If demand for small fish remains strong, restrictions in one market may redirect effort or increase pressure elsewhere.

For Japan, stock-specific management is essential because Pacific and Tsushima Current stocks experience different environments, migration routes, age structures, and fisheries. The 2019 review emphasizes management strategy evaluation, fishery-independent monitoring, and international coordination around the East China Sea, Yellow Sea, and Japan Sea ([Yatsu review](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12562-019-01305-3)).

For the eastern Pacific, U.S. and Mexican management should preserve the transboundary stock framework while improving distribution, age, and price information. The 70% U.S.-water assumption is useful for a harvest rule but should not be mistaken for an annual observation.

For all markets, quality management is economic management. Rapid chilling, stable freezing, traceability, and oxidation and histamine controls protect the value of the biological resource after capture. A fishery can have adequate biomass yet lose market value through poor cold-chain performance; conversely, a high price can reflect scarcity or trade disruption rather than improved biological quality.

## Closing judgment

Chub mackerel links the marine environment, fish biology, fisheries economics, and markets through a real but unevenly measured system. The best-supported biological chain runs from currents, temperature, productivity, and prey to growth, recruitment, distribution, condition, and biomass. The best-supported economic chain runs from biomass and catch composition through fishing effort, grades, exports, inventories, and prices. South Korea provides the clearest example of these chains meeting: a new export outlet for small fish coincided with a shift toward a nearby, small-fish fishing ground, while the biological evidence did not require a population-wide collapse in size at age.

The evidence does not justify a single Pacific Rim price ranking or a direct claim that ocean temperature caused a particular market price. It does justify species-resolved market statistics, stock-specific biological comparisons, lagged environmental analysis, and management that treats market demand and fishing-ground selection as part of the ecological system.
